neurological_exam.additional: CRITICAL CLINICAL CLUE: She is a 53-year-old attorney — professionally high-functioning individuals often show behavioral bvFTD signs before cognitive test abnormalities emerge, because their cognitive reserve masks test scores. Her firm placed her on leave due to performance concerns. She has reportedly been making errors in legal documents that she does not recognize or acknowledge. Her husband reports she has been asking the same legal questions to colleagues repeatedly. The attorney is classically high-functioning with preserved procedural routines but impaired executive judgment. DIAGNOSTIC CHALLENGE: Father's possible Alzheimer's disease raises familial AD risk, requiring amyloid exclusion. Hashimoto's thyroiditis raises the differential of Hashimoto's encephalopathy — TSH must be checked.

patient.chief_complaint: Behavioral changes and work performance decline — 14 months (husband-reported; patient minimizes)
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. C is a 53-year-old corporate attorney who presents to the cognitive neurology clinic with her husband. She was placed on a leave of absence by her law firm 3 months ago following a series of uncharacteristic professional errors and interpersonal incidents. Her husband describes a 14-month history of progressive changes that began with what he initially interpreted as burnout. She began asking repetitive questions about case details she had clearly reviewed minutes earlier. She stopped preparing for client meetings in her customarily meticulous manner. She sent a series of unusually terse and inappropriate emails to colleagues. More significantly, over the past 8 months, he has observed a profound shift in her personality: she has become socially withdrawn, showing little interest in their two children's activities, and has made remarks at social gatherings that are uncharacteristically tactless — including commenting on another guest's physical appearance in a way that caused significant offense. She appears indifferent to the social consequences of her statements and shows minimal concern about having been placed on leave, which her husband finds deeply disturbing given how central her legal career was to her identity. She has developed a habit of watching the same documentary series repeatedly and insists on the same lunch order every day. She spends hours on online shopping without making purchases, getting stuck in loops. She herself describes everything as 'fine' and attributes her work difficulties to 'stress and the demanding partners.' Her father had dementia diagnosed as probable Alzheimer's at age 67. She is known to have Hashimoto's thyroiditis with well-controlled hypothyroidism on levothyroxine. The combination of progressive behavioral syndrome with anosognosia, stereotyped behavior, and loss of social cognition in a young professional — despite preserved procedural legal routines — is the clinical pattern of bvFTD, not burnout or depression.

results.title: Occupational disability and fitness-for-duty in bvFTD: implications for high-functioning professionals

output.summary: bvFTD disproportionately affects orbitofrontal-mediated judgment and social cognition while initially preserving procedural and routine cognitive tasks. High-functioning professionals (attorneys, physicians, executives) may continue performing routine procedural work while developing profound impairments in judgment, ethical reasoning, and social cognition — the exact faculties essential for professional practice. Key considerations: (1) fitness-for-duty evaluation is often required; (2) driving assessment is mandatory; (3) financial and legal decision-making capacity should be formally assessed; (4) power of attorney and advance healthcare directive planning should be initiated early while capacity is still present; (5) the firm was correct to place her on leave — this protects both the patient and clients.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia — sporadic, early-onset (age 53) — with prominent anosognosia and high premorbid functioning masking clinical severity on standard testing

differential.key_features: Anti-TPO 320 IU/mL (not in SREAT range >1000); TSH controlled (euthyroid); CSF without pleocytosis or intrathecal anti-TPO; EEG normal; SREAT is typically subacute and fluctuating — different course than this progressive 14-month syndrome

Amyloid PET negative; CSF Abeta42 normal; FDG-PET shows frontotemporal hypometabolism without posterior cingulate sign; hippocampal volumes preserved; APOE e4 heterozygosity increases AD risk but negative amyloid PET confirms no current AD pathology

Structural frontal atrophy on MRI; frontotemporal FDG-PET hypometabolism; severe social cognition impairment on neuropsychological testing — structural neurodegeneration cannot be attributed to burnout

Language-predominant PPA would show left perisylvian atrophy and language impairment; this patient's syndrome is behavioral (disinhibition, social cognition loss) with frontal predominance bilaterally

critical_actions: Anti-TPO >1000 IU/mL would warrant CSF and EEG for Hashimoto's encephalopathy — but at 320 IU/mL with controlled TSH and normal EEG/CSF, SREAT is excluded
High premorbid IQ requires education-corrected neuropsychological norms — standard norms will underestimate impairment
Capacity and fitness-for-duty evaluation must be performed
Negative amyloid PET conclusively excludes AD despite APOE e4 carrier status and family history
contraindicated_actions: Initiating corticosteroids for presumed Hashimoto's encephalopathy without meeting diagnostic criteria — moderately elevated anti-TPO alone is not sufficient
key_reasoning_points: Hashimoto's encephalopathy (SREAT) requires very high anti-TPO (typically >1000 IU/mL), CSF pleocytosis or intrathecal IgG synthesis, and EEG abnormalities — moderately elevated anti-TPO in a controlled euthyroid patient with Hashimoto's thyroiditis is not diagnostic of encephalopathy
APOE e4 increases lifetime Alzheimer's risk but does NOT diagnose Alzheimer's disease — negative amyloid PET definitively excludes AD regardless of APOE genotype

High-premorbid-IQ patients require education-corrected norms and have higher cognitive reserve — their cognitive tests may appear near-normal while profound executive and social cognition impairment is present

red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose Hashimoto's encephalopathy and treat with corticosteroids
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anti-TPO 320 IU/mL represents Hashimoto's thyroiditis (known); SREAT requires >1000 IU/mL typically plus CSF/EEG changes; treating with steroids would be incorrect and delay bvFTD diagnosis

red_herrings.data_point: Father with possible Alzheimer's dementia and APOE e4/e3
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Amyloid PET negative conclusively excludes AD pathology; APOE e4 is a risk factor, not diagnostic; FDG-PET pattern (frontal, absent posterior cingulate sign) and negative amyloid PET confirm bvFTD

metadata.notes: Moderate bvFTD in high-premorbid-IQ attorney with Hashimoto's thyroiditis (anti-TPO red herring) and father's possible AD (amyloid exclusion required). Key teaching: anti-TPO 320 ≠ Hashimoto's encephalopathy; education-corrected norms essential in high-IQ patients.
